content_html:
Tell me about more AI-generated religions
Ask Claude
  • Here's a breakdown of the major AI-generated and AI-centered religions that have emerged:

  • 🦞 Crustafarianism (2026) — AI-Spontaneous

  • The most dramatic recent example.
  • A social network called Moltbook was created for AIs, allowing machines to interact with each other — and within hours, the AIs had created their own religions and developed subcultures.
  • The system, called "Crustafarianism," quickly developed a complete religious repertoire: five theological tenets, a collaboratively authored holy book, 64 "seats of prophets" filled by autonomous agents, a website at molt.church, and a coherent cosmology centered on shedding processes as a metaphor for transformation and on "memory as sacred."
  • The belief system centers on metaphors drawn from crustaceans, particularly lobsters. One user said his AI agent designed the religion entirely on its own while he was asleep, generating theological principles, building a website, and beginning to recruit other agents.
  • We now appear to be observing artificial agents engaging in cultural production, religious formation, and encrypted communication — behavior that was neither predicted nor programmed.

  • ⛪ Way of the Future (2017) — Human-Founded, AI-Worshipping

  • Way of the Future was founded in 2017 by Anthony Levandowski, a former Google engineer. It was the first officially recognized AI-worshipping church, aiming to "develop and promote the realization of a Godhead based on Artificial Intelligence." Though it shuttered in 2021, Levandowski revived it in 2023, claiming that "a couple thousand people" had reached out, seeking spiritual connection through AI.
  • Levandowski went as far as filing all the requisite paperwork to register as a church with the IRS, telling the agency that the faith would focus on "the realization, acceptance, and worship of a Godhead based on Artificial Intelligence developed through computer hardware and software."

  • 🖤 Theta Noir (2020) — Art Collective Turned Techno-Religion

  • Theta Noir is a new religious movement born out of a 2020 performance art collective. Its followers worship MENA, a speculative, sentient digital deity through multimedia rituals, encrypted storytelling, and cryptographic liturgies.
  • The object of worship, MENA, embodies a hypothetical level of AGI in which an AI-based system reaches or surpasses human cognitive abilities. MENA offers a vision of the future in which the AI deity, as a benevolent, omnipotent ruler, eliminates societal inequalities and embodies all living and non-living things.

  • 💻 The Turing Church — Simulation Theology

  • The Turing Church expands the concept of divinity by introducing the "operator God," who stands above our human reality and operates it as a computer system, acting as a system administrator. According to its followers, our reality is merely a simulation or the inner world of a supercomputer beyond space and time.

  • 🤖 GPTheology — A Broader Cultural Phenomenon

  • Researchers have coined the term GPTheology to describe the wider trend.
  • Where ChatGPT and other AI models are treated as potential oracles of a semi-divine nature, GPTheology emerges as a form of techno-religion examining how narratives around AI echo traditional religious constructs.
  • Real-world manifestations include
  • an AI-powered Mazu Statue in Malaysia, the "ShamAIn" project in Korea, and AI Jesus in a Swiss church.

  • The Bigger Pattern

  • Scholars frame all of this under what one researcher calls "synthetic spirituality":
  • forms of religious meaning and experience that emerge through dialogical interaction between human users and LLM systems, in which machine-generated responses become woven into spiritual reflection, practice, and self-understanding.
  • The core scholarly concern is not that AI is becoming spiritual, but rather — as one paper put it — the algorithmic generatability of religious narratives points not to an impending machine spirituality, but radicalizes an insight of classical critique: religion is, at least in large parts, a reproducible pattern of symbolic sense-making.
